en: The Pāli Canon: Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga Nissaggiyakaṇḍa (The Section on Forfeiture in the Great Analysis of the Monastic Code)
The Chapter on the Groups:
25. The Training Rule on Taking Away a Robe.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son said this to a bhikkhu who was a co-resident disciple of his brother:
"Come, friend, let us set out on a tour of the countryside.
"I will not go, venerable sir."
“I have weak robes.
“Come, friend, I will give you a robe,” he said,
and gave him a robe.
That bhikkhu heard:
"The Blessed One, it is said, will set out on a tour of the countryside.
Then this thought occurred to that bhikkhu:
“I will not set out on a tour of the countryside together with the venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son; I will set out on a tour of the countryside together with the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son said this to that bhikkhu:
“Come now, friend, let us set out on a tour of the countryside.”
“Venerable sir, I will not set out on a tour of the countryside with you; I will set out on a tour of the countryside with the Blessed One.
“Friend, as for that robe I gave you, thinking you would set out on a tour of the countryside with me,” he said, and being angry and displeased, he tore it away.
Then that bhikkhu reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before]... were indignant, disparaged it, and complained about it, saying:
"How can Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son, having personally given a robe to a bhikkhu, later take it back in anger and displeasure?"
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true,
Upananda, that after giving a robe to a bhikkhu yourself, you took it back in anger and displeasure?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, having personally given a robe to a bhikkhu, take it back while angry and displeased?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“Whatever monk, having himself given a robe to another monk, being angry and displeased, should take it back or cause it to be taken back, incurs an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
“Whatever monk” means:
Whoever is such a person … [and so on] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is what is intended by the term “bhikkhu” in this context.
"Of a bhikkhu" means: of another bhikkhu. "His own" (sāmaṃ) means: [his own].
Having given it oneself.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes; the last one is that which is subject to assignment.
"Purchased with an unhappy mind" means being dissatisfied, with a wounded heart, and full of resentment.
"Should take away" means...
If she herself seizes it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she causes another to seize it by commanding them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, having been instructed once, he takes back even much [cloth], it is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be relinquished:
…pe… “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which I gave to a bhikkhu myself and then took back, is an article to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
…pe… “He should give it,” …pe…
"May he give... ... [and so on] ... "I give it to the Venerable One.

Having given a robe to one who is ordained while perceiving him as ordained, if he—being angry and displeased—takes it back or causes it to be taken back, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If one has given a robe to one who is fully ordained, and being doubtful, one—angry and displeased—takes it back or causes it to be taken back, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If one has given a robe to one who is fully ordained, perceiving them as not fully ordained, and being angry and displeased, one takes it back or causes it to be taken back, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one gives another requisite and, being angry and displeased, takes it back or causes it to be taken back, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If, having given a robe or another requisite to one who is not fully ordained, one becomes angry and displeased and either takes it back or causes it to be taken back, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is in doubt regarding a person who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives someone who is not fully ordained as not being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if he gives it himself.
Or he takes it with confidence from him;
or [the giver] is insane;
or he is a first-time offender.
The fifth training rule concerning the snatching away of robes is finished.
